pairings.why: The bitterness cuts through the fried coating and the citrus hops pick up the curry leaf and green chilli.
Char on the paneer meets the caramel note in the malt, while the hops lift the smoky marinade.
Firm bitterness stands up to the tangy, nutty gravy without the chilli taking over.
The malt sweetness echoes the ghee-roasted carrot and the dry finish keeps the pudding from feeling heavy.

tastes:
Pour one and the hops arrive first: grapefruit peel, orange, a bit of pine, sometimes a floral edge. Underneath sits a pale, biscuity malt base with a touch of caramel, enough to carry the bitterness without turning sweet. The finish is dry and firm. It should leave you wanting a second sip rather than a glass of water.

The style took shape in California around 1980, when small brewers started using Cascade, a then-new American hop, in a beer built on the English pale ale template. Swap the earthy English hops for loud citrus ones, swap the fruity English yeast for a clean American strain. Then you have it. Later hops such as Centennial, Citra and Simcoe pushed it further towards tropical fruit.

What keeps it distinct from an IPA is restraint. It is lighter in alcohol, lighter in bitterness and more balanced, so the malt still has a say. A good one is the beer you order when you want flavour but plan to stay a while.
